title: Code the pattern
goal: I can find the rule for the nth term of a pattern and use it for the 100th term. I can test my rule with a loop.

learn.intro: A rule for the nth term jumps straight to any term, such as the 100th. The difference tells you which times table to compare with. A loop in code adds the difference again and again, so you can test your rule.

example.problem: Find the rule for the nth term of 9, 14, 19, 24, ... Then find the 100th term.
steps: The difference is 5, so compare each term with the 5 times table.
Each term is 4 more than the number above it. The rule is 5n + 4.
Test it in code: set term to 9, then repeat 99 times: change term by 5. The 100th term is 99 jumps after the 1st term.
example.answer: The rule is 5n + 4. The 100th term is 504.

howto.title: How to find the rule for the nth term
steps: Find the difference between neighbouring terms.
Write that times table under n: 5, 10, 15, ...
Find how much to add or take away to reach each term.
Check the rule on 2 terms. Then use it for any term.

try.text: A sequence starts 3, 10, 17, 24, ... The rule for the nth term is {b} × n − {b}. The 100th term is {b}.
try.explanation: The difference is 7, so compare with 7, 14, 21, 28. Each term is 4 less than the number under it. The rule is 7n − 4. The 100th term is 7 × 100 − 4 = 696.

items.text: Matchsticks make 2 rows of squares. Each new pattern adds one more column of 2 squares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Pattern 3 has {b} sticks. Each new column adds {b} sticks.

items.explanation: Count: pattern 1 has 7 sticks, pattern 2 has 12, pattern 3 has 17. Each new column adds 5 sticks, so the rule is 5n + 2 (5 × 1 + 2 = 7). Pattern 40: 5 × 40 + 2 = 202. For 92 sticks: 5n + 2 = 92, so 5n = 90 and n = 18.

items.text: For each sequence, fill in the difference, the rule for the nth term and the 100th term.
items.explanation: (a) The difference is 6. Compare with 6, 12, 18, 24: each term is 2 more, so 6n + 2 and 6 × 100 + 2 = 602. (b) The difference is 5. Each term is 2 less than 5, 10, 15, 20, so 5n − 2 and 5 × 100 − 2 = 498.

items.text: A sequence has the rule 5n + 2. Its first terms are 7, 12, 17, 22, ...

parts.label: a
parts.text: Is 157 a term?  {circ:Yes|No}   If yes, it is term number {b}.

items.explanation: (a) 157 − 2 = 155 = 5 × 31, so 157 is the 31st term. (b) 205 − 2 = 203 is not a multiple of 5. The terms end in 2 or 7, so 205 is not one. (c) 5 × 60 + 2 = 302.

items.text: Trace the code. The sprite says x first, then changes it. Fill in the trace table.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The last number it says is {b}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When the program ends, x is {b}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: With repeat 50, the last number it says is {b}.

items.explanation: Loop 1: it says 3, then x becomes 9. Loop 2: says 9, x becomes 15. Loop 3: says 15, x becomes 21. Loop 4: says 21, x becomes 27. The last number said is 21 but x ends as 27. With repeat 50 it says the 1st term, then 49 jumps later it says 3 + 49 × 6 = 297.

items.text: Complete the code so that the sprite says the first 15 terms of 11, 18, 25, 32, ...

parts.label: d
parts.text: The last number it says is {b}.

items.explanation: The 1st term is 11, so set n to 11. Each jump adds 7. The sprite says a term, then changes n, and 15 terms need 15 says: repeat 15. The last number said is the 15th term: 7 × 15 + 4 = 109.

items.text: Siti's code should say the 30th term of 4, 9, 14, 19, ...

parts.label: c
parts.text: To fix it, change repeat 30 to repeat {b}.

items.explanation: The loop adds 5 thirty times: 4 + 5 × 30 = 154. That is the 31st term. The 30th term is 5 × 30 − 1 = 149. From the 1st to the 30th term there are only 29 jumps, so use repeat 29.

items.text: Ali has $15 on Day 1. Every day after that he adds $7. So on Day 2 he has $22.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Money on Day n = {b} × n + {b} dollars.

parts.label: d
parts.text: He first has more than $200 on Day {b}.

items.explanation: Each day adds $7, so the rule is 7n + 8 (7 × 1 + 8 = 15). (a) Day 4: 7 × 4 + 8 = 36. (c) Day 30: 7 × 30 + 8 = 218. (d) 7n + 8 is more than 200 when 7n is more than 192. 7 × 27 = 189 is too small, 7 × 28 = 196 works: Day 28 (he has $204).

items.text: Circle the rule that gives each sequence. Test n = 1 and n = 2.
items.explanation: Put n = 1 and n = 2 into each rule. (a) 5 × 1 − 1 = 4 and 5 × 2 − 1 = 9. (b) 3 × 1 + 7 = 10 and 3 × 2 + 7 = 13. (c) 8 × 1 − 5 = 3 and 8 × 2 − 5 = 11. The other rules fail on the 1st term.

items.text: A loop starts at the 1st term of a sequence. Each repeat moves on to the next term.

parts.label: a
parts.text: To reach the 60th term, repeat {b} times.

parts.label: b
parts.text: After repeat 40, the sprite is at term number {b}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: To go from the 8th term to the 25th term, repeat {b} times.

items.explanation: The 1st term needs 0 repeats and each repeat adds 1 to the term number. (a) 60 − 1 = 59 repeats. (b) 1 + 40 = the 41st term. (c) 25 − 8 = 17 repeats. The repeats count the jumps, not the terms.

items.text: This code uses n as a counter and says a rule. Predict what it says.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The first 3 numbers it says are {b}, {b}, {b}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The last number it says is {b}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: To say 5, 9, 13, 17, ... change the rule to {b} × n + {b}.

items.text: Use the rules to find terms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In 6n + 1, the number 61 is term number {b}.

parts.label: d
parts.text: In 9n − 4, the number 158 is term number {b}.

items.text: A sequence goes up by the same amount each time. Its 4th term is 23 and its 9th term is 53.

parts.label: a
parts.text: From the 4th term to the 9th term is {b} jumps.

items.explanation: From the 4th to the 9th term is 9 − 4 = 5 jumps. The terms rose by 30, so each jump is 30 ÷ 5 = 6. Going back 3 jumps from the 4th term: 23 − 18 = 5. The rule is 6n − 1 (6 × 4 − 1 = 23).

items.text: Aisha looks at 2, 8, 14, 20, ... The difference is 6, so she says the rule is 6n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rule 6n gives {b} for the 1st term, but the 1st term is {b}.

items.explanation: The rule 6n gives 6 for the 1st term, but the 1st term is 2. Each term is 4 less than 6n: 6 − 4 = 2, 12 − 4 = 8. The difference only tells you the times table. You must still compare with the terms.

items.text: A sequence goes down by the same amount each time: 58, 53, 48, 43, ...

parts.label: a
parts.text: The rule for the nth term is {b} − 5n.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The last term above 0 is term number {b}.

items.hint: The terms go down by 5. Take 5 × n away from a start number.
items.explanation: (a) The terms go down by 5, so take 5n from a number. 5 × 1 = 5 and 58 + 5 = 63, so the rule is 63 − 5n. (b) 63 − 50 = 13. (c) 63 − 5n stays above 0 while 5n is less than 63. 5 × 12 = 60 gives 3 and 5 × 13 = 65 would be below 0, so term 12.

items.text: Program P starts at the 1st term of 6, 10, 14, 18, ... Program Q starts at the 5th term of the same sequence. Both change by 4 each repeat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: To end at the same term, P must repeat {b} times.

items.hint: Count how many terms Q moves on. P starts 4 terms earlier.
items.explanation: The 5th term is 4 × 5 + 2 = 22. Q adds 4 sixteen times: 22 + 64 = 86. Q has moved 16 terms on, so it ends at term 5 + 16 = 21. P starts at the 1st term, so it needs 21 − 1 = 20 repeats. Check: 6 + 20 × 4 = 86.

items.text: The nth term of a sequence is 9n + 4.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The number of terms that are less than 300 is {b}.

items.hint: Try n = 50 first. Then move up or down until you are close.
items.explanation: (a) 9n + 4 is near 500 when n is near 55: 9 × 55 + 4 = 499 and 9 × 56 + 4 = 508. 499 is only 1 away from 500. (b) It is the 55th term. (c) 9n + 4 is less than 300 while 9n is less than 296. 9 × 32 = 288 works and 9 × 33 = 297 does not, so 32 terms.

items.text:
Beyond Level 6: Second differences.
Matchsticks make staircases. Staircase 1 has 1 square, staircase 2 has 3 squares and staircase 3 has 6 squares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Count the sticks. Staircase 2 has {b} and staircase 3 has {b}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The extra sticks go up by the same amount each time. Staircase 4 has {b} sticks and staircase 5 has {b}.

items.hint: Find how many extra sticks each staircase adds. Look for a pattern.
items.explanation: The extra sticks each time are 6 (4 to 10), then 8 (10 to 18). They go up by 2 each time, so the next extras are 10 and 12: 18 + 10 = 28 and 28 + 12 = 40. For staircase 10 add the extras 6, 8, ..., 22 to 4: 4 + 126 = 130. (The rule is n × n + 3n, a rule that is not a times table plus a number.)

items.text: A sprite says these numbers in order: 3, 20, 7, 25, 11, 30, 15, 35, ...

parts.label: a
parts.text: Places 1, 3, 5, ... go up by {b}. Places 2, 4, 6, ... go up by {b}.

items.hint: Split it into two sequences. Which one is place 15 in?
items.explanation: Places 1, 3, 5, ... say 3, 7, 11, 15: they go up by 4. Places 2, 4, 6, ... say 20, 25, 30, 35: they go up by 5. Place 15 is the 8th of the first kind: 3 + 7 × 4 = 31. Place 20 is the 10th of the second kind: 20 + 9 × 5 = 65. 60 is in the second kind: 20 + 8 × 5 = 60 is its 9th number, which is place 18.

items.text: A sequence has the rule 6n − 2. Plan a program that starts at the 1st term and says the 40th term.

parts.label: c
parts.text: set n to {b}, then repeat {b} [change n by {b}], then say n.

items.hint: How many jumps are there from the 1st term to the 40th term?
items.explanation: n = 1, 2, 3, 4 give 4, 10, 16, 22. The 40th term is 6 × 40 − 2 = 238. The program starts at the 1st term, 4, and jumps 6 each time. From the 1st to the 40th term there are 39 jumps, so: set n to 4, repeat 39 [change n by 6], say n.

items.text:
Beyond Level 6: Triangle numbers.
What does this code say? Write t after each repeat.
items.hint: Write t after every repeat: 1, 3, 6, ... Where does it pass 100?
items.explanation: t after each repeat: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 45, 55, 66, 78, 91, 105. The repeat stops the first time t is above 100, which is after repeat 14, so k is 14 and t is 105. (These are the triangle numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, ... : the extra amount is 1 more each time.)

items.text: Find the rule for 9, 16, 23, 30, ... The rule is {b} × n + {b}. The 100th term is {b}.
items.explanation: The difference is 7. Each term is 2 more than 7, 14, 21, 28, so the rule is 7n + 2. The 100th term is 7 × 100 + 2 = 702.

items.text: Is 125 a term of 7, 12, 17, 22, ...?  {circ:Yes|No}
items.explanation: The rule is 5n + 2. 125 − 2 = 123 is not a multiple of 5. The terms end in 2 or 7, so 125 is not a term.

items.text: Predict what the code says.
items.explanation: 8 + 20 × 6 = 128. From the 1st term to the 21st term there are 20 jumps, so 128 is the 21st term. Check: 6 × 21 + 2 = 128.

items.text: Mei wants the first 4 terms of 5, 8, 11, 14. What does her code say?

parts.label: b
parts.text: The number it never says is {b}.

items.explanation: Each loop changes n first, so it says 8, 11, 14, 17. The 1st term 5 is never said, and 17 is one term too far. To fix it, swap the 2 blocks inside the repeat.
